proposed_edges.evidence_note: Freshly read publisher title page in ETH Library’s four-page front-matter scan, PDF p. 1: “EDITED BY” precedes all four names and the 2010 Belknap Press imprint. Contents on PDF pp. 2–4 allocate separate chapters. Bibliographic collaboration only; the introduction and chapter bodies remain unread. Existing source hc177_ferguson_shock is reused. proposed_edges.relationship: In “Embracing Fearlessness” (2019), J. R. McNeill names Maier among his important graduate mentors at Duke and credits his engagement with twentieth-century European history.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Fresh primary interview, Allison Miller, Perspectives on History 57:1 (January 2019), printed p. 27, PDF p. 29, answer on early mentors: “the most important figures for me were probably Charles Maier” and John Cell; Maier mattered for “the depth of his engagement with 20th-century European history”. McNeill’s own retrospective testimony supports a bounded mentorship/influence edge. It does not identify a formal dissertation supervisor or make Maier the source of McNeill’s environmental method. The subsequent team-teaching and intellectual liberation concern John Cell, not Maier. Printed pp. 26–28 were read through the official issue PDF; the HTML version returned 403.

proposed_edges.relationship: Maier and Sven Beckert jointly founded the Weatherhead Initiative on Global History (2012) and are named as joint moderators of its Approaches to Global History seminar in a 2015 programme.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Fresh institutional About page, “About WIGH”, first and final paragraphs: the initiative “was founded in 2012” by the two historians, who are also named as co-chairs. The dated Graduate Student Presentations programme, 4 May 2015, paragraph beginning “This graduate-faculty research seminar”, identifies History 2950hf, Approaches to Global History, and says discussions “will be moderated by Professors Sven Beckert and Charles S. Maier”. This is a documented joint research/teaching undertaking, recorded undirected; the programme documents announced roles, not a verified transcript of that meeting. No co-authored theoretical position, chapter allocation, or reciprocal personal influence is inferred. The course papers remain unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: In “Hot Memory … Cold Memory” (2002; delivered 2001), Maier offers a speculative explanation of the differing persistence of Nazi and Communist memories.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: New primary evidence for the held memory relationship: online sections I, IV and V, especially the definition, terror comparison and final qualification “very speculative hypothesis”. Western scope; explanatory hypothesis, no ranking of atrocities. Newsletter pp. 1, 5 verifies March 2001 delivery; online footer dates publication 2002. The earlier research statement remains unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: In “Hot Memory … Cold Memory” (2002; delivered 2001), Maier tentatively aligns his inquiry with Paul Ricœur’s conference call to move from melancholy to mourning.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Primary section V, final paragraph: Maier names Ricœur’s opening address and suggests his paper contributes to that exercise. Bounded acknowledgment; Ricœur’s original address unread. Newsletter p. 1 independently dates his opening to 9 March 2001.
